topic: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
title: Relationships, sexuality and parenting
blurb: Support the right of people with a learning disability to relationships, sex and parenthood, while applying the law on capacity and protection.
question: Lily, 25, has a learning disability and a new boyfriend. Her mother asks the team to assess whether Lily can consent to a sexual relationship. Following A Local Authority v JB (2021), what must Lily be able to understand about the other person?

teach.h: Relationships are a right, not a privilege
teach.body: People with a learning disability have the same right to friendships, intimate relationships, sex, marriage and family life as anyone else. Article 8 of the Human Rights Act protects private and family life, and Article 23 of the UN CRPD requires states to end discrimination in marriage, family, parenthood and relationships. In plain English: the nurse's job is to support relationships safely, not to prevent them because of the disability.

teach.h: Some decisions can never be made for someone
teach.body: Section 27 of the Mental Capacity Act lists decisions that nobody can make on behalf of a person who lacks capacity, including consenting to marriage or civil partnership and consenting to sexual relations. So there is no 'best interests' consent to sex. Capacity is presumed, assessed for the specific decision, and supported with accessible information first.

steps.label: Relevant information
steps.sub: Includes that the other person must be able to consent

teach.caption: A Local Authority v JB [2021] UKSC 52.

teach.body: Lily, 25, has a learning disability and a new boyfriend. Her mother is worried. The nurse starts from the presumption of capacity and, with the community team, offers Lily accessible sex and relationships sessions using pictures and repetition. If an assessment is needed, it covers the relevant information, including that her partner must be able to consent and must give and keep giving consent. Her mother's views are heard, but they do not decide Lily's capacity.

head: Situation
Supportive response
rows: Accessible information; support to a clinic
Support it; talk about safety and consent
Hear them; the adult decides if capable
Assess capacity for marriage if in doubt

rows.label: SOA 2003 s38
values: Care worker sexual activity is an offence

teach.body: Many people with a learning disability are good parents with the right support. CRPD Article 23 requires appropriate assistance with child-rearing and says a child must never be separated from parents because of a parent's disability. The child's welfare comes first, so real concerns are acted on, but a learning disability alone is not a reason for a child protection referral. Start by assessing support needs and offering adapted, practical teaching.

teach.caption: Repetition and positive reinforcement are named NMC communication skills (Annexe A).

teach.text: Two opposite errors. One: stopping relationships or sex education 'to keep the person safe' (this breaches their rights and leaves them less able to recognise abuse). Two: treating a care worker's relationship with a person they support as a private matter (it is a likely offence under SOA 2003 s38 whatever the person says).

items: Relationships, sex and parenthood are rights (Article 8; CRPD Article 23).
MCA s27: nobody can consent to sex or marriage on another's behalf.
JB (2021): understanding that the other person must be able to consent and consent throughout.
Care worker sexual activity with a person they support is an offence (SOA s38).
Parents with LD: assess support needs and teach practically; disability alone is not a reason to separate.

summary: You can now support relationships and sexuality as rights, apply the presumption of capacity and the JB test, and recognise when the law protects people from exploitation. You can also plan adapted support for parents with a learning disability.

A.q: Paul, 31, has a mild learning disability and lives in supported living. He tells his keyworker he has a girlfriend he met at college. A support worker suggests stopping the relationship 'to keep him safe'. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Agree, and ask his parents to decide about the relationship
Support it, as Paul has the same right to relationships as anyone
Allow it if staff supervise all of their time together
Refer Paul for a capacity assessment before he sees her
A.why: Article 8 and CRPD Article 23 protect relationships. Capacity is presumed (MCA s1(2)); staff should support the relationship and talk with Paul about safety and consent.

whyNot.0: His parents cannot decide his relationships for him.
whyNot.2: Supervising all contact is an unjustified interference with his private life.
whyNot.3: Capacity is presumed; there is no reason given to doubt it here.

A.q: A nurse is preparing to assess whether Lily, 25, who has a learning disability, has capacity to decide to engage in sexual relations. Following A Local Authority v JB (2021), what must the relevant information include?
options: That the other person must be able to consent and consent throughout
That her parents must agree to the relationship beforehand
That they must be married or in a civil partnership first
That her partner must be known to her support team
A.why: JB [2021] UKSC 52: the relevant information includes that the other person must have the capacity to consent and must consent before and throughout the sexual activity.

whyNot.1: Parental agreement is not part of the test for an adult.
whyNot.2: Marriage is not required for lawful consensual sex and is not part of the test.
whyNot.3: The support team's knowledge of her partner is not part of the relevant information.

A.q: Tom, 30, has a severe learning disability and has been assessed as lacking capacity to consent to sexual relations. His father asks whether he can consent on Tom's behalf, in Tom's best interests. What is the correct answer?
options: Yes, as his father and nearest relative
Yes, after a best interests meeting
No, but a deputy appointed by the court could
No, the MCA bars anyone consenting for him
A.why: MCA s27: consent to sexual relations is one of the decisions that nobody can make on behalf of a person who lacks capacity.

whyNot.0: Being a parent gives no power to consent to sex for an adult.
whyNot.1: Best interests decisions cannot be made about consent to sexual relations.
whyNot.2: A deputy cannot make s27 decisions either.

B.q: Mia, 19, has a mild learning disability and asks her community nurse about contraception because she has a new boyfriend. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Tell her she must discuss it with her parents first
Advise her to wait until her boyfriend is assessed
Give accessible information and support her to a clinic
Arrange a capacity assessment before any discussion
B.why: Mia is an adult with a right to sexual health care. Capacity is presumed; accessible information and support to attend a clinic are reasonable adjustments.

whyNot.0: As an adult she does not need parental involvement.
whyNot.1: Her boyfriend's assessment is not a condition of her care.
whyNot.3: There is no reason to doubt her capacity, and information should come first.

B.q: Staff report that Sam, 30, who has a severe learning disability and lives in a group home, has started masturbating in the shared lounge. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Support him to learn that his bedroom is a private place for this
Ask the GP to prescribe medication to reduce his sex drive
Keep him out of the lounge when other residents are there
Record it as sexual abuse of the other residents
B.why: Masturbation is a normal behaviour. The aim is to teach private and public places, using his communication methods and consistent prompts.

whyNot.1: Medication to suppress sexuality is a restrictive and inappropriate first response.
whyNot.2: Excluding him restricts him without teaching the skill he needs.
whyNot.3: This mislabels a teaching need, though staff should consider the impact on others.

B.q: Zoe, 26, has a moderate learning disability and plans to marry her partner. Her parents ask the nurse to stop the wedding because they doubt she understands marriage. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Ask her parents to give consent to the marriage for her
Support an accessible assessment of her capacity to marry
Advise her to delay until she is aged 30 or more
Arrange a best interests meeting to decide about the wedding
B.why: Capacity is presumed and decision-specific. If there is real doubt, her capacity to marry is assessed with accessible information. Nobody can consent to marriage on her behalf (MCA s27).

whyNot.0: Parents cannot consent to marriage for an adult.
whyNot.2: There is no age rule for people with a learning disability; this would be discriminatory.
whyNot.3: Marriage cannot be decided by a best interests process (s27).

C.q: Sasha, 24, has a mild learning disability and is 20 weeks pregnant. A professional suggests a referral to children's social care 'because of her learning disability'. There are no other concerns. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Make the referral now, as learning disability is a risk factor
Wait until the birth and then reassess her parenting
Assess her support needs as a parent and offer adapted support
Ask her mother to agree to care for the baby
C.why: Disability alone is not grounds for child protection action (CRPD Art 23(4)). Assessing support needs and offering adapted antenatal and parenting support is the appropriate response; real concerns would still be acted on.

whyNot.0: Referring because of disability alone is discriminatory.
whyNot.1: Waiting misses the chance to plan support during pregnancy.
whyNot.3: This assumes Sasha cannot parent without any assessment.

C.q: A student asks what the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities says about parents with a disability. Which statement is accurate?
options: A child must not be separated from parents because of a parent's disability
Parents with a learning disability need a court order to keep a child
Parents with a disability are assessed by a specialist before birth
Parents with a disability may choose adoption with state support
C.why: CRPD Article 23(4): in no case shall a child be separated from parents on the basis of a disability of the child or one or both parents. Article 23(2) requires appropriate assistance with child-rearing.

whyNot.1: No such requirement exists, and it would be discriminatory.
whyNot.2: The CRPD does not require a pre-birth specialist assessment of disabled parents.
whyNot.3: This is not what Article 23 says; it focuses on support to parent and not separating families because of disability.

C.q: Sasha has just had her first baby and is learning to make up formula feeds safely before going home. Which teaching approach is most appropriate?
options: Give her the standard leaflet to read at home
Show the steps practically with pictures and repeat them
Explain the steps once in detail before discharge
Ask her partner to learn so that he can do the feeds
C.why: Practical demonstration, picture step cards, practice and repetition with positive feedback suit how many people with a learning disability learn best.

whyNot.0: A standard leaflet may not be accessible to her.
whyNot.2: A single verbal explanation is unlikely to be retained.
whyNot.3: This removes her role as a parent instead of supporting her to learn.

reteach.title: Support first, protect where the law requires
reteach.question: How do you balance a person's right to relationships with keeping them safe?

blocks.body: Start with the right: relationships, sex and parenthood belong to everyone. Next, presume capacity and teach before assessing. Then apply the protections: nobody consents to sex or marriage for someone else, care workers must not have sexual contact with people they support, and real abuse is raised under safeguarding.

blocks.text: There is no 'best interests' consent to sex or marriage: MCA s27 rules it out.

explain.body: Article 8 protects private and family life. CRPD Article 23 covers marriage, family, parenthood and relationships on an equal basis. Staff support relationships and teach safety; they do not stop them because of disability.

test.q: Which Human Rights Act article most directly protects the relationships of a person with a learning disability?
options: Article 5
Article 3
Article 2
Article 8
test.why: Article 8 protects private and family life, including relationships.

whyNot.1: Article 3 concerns inhuman or degrading treatment.
whyNot.2: Article 2 concerns the right to life.

explain.body: Capacity is presumed and decision-specific. JB (2021): the relevant information includes that the other person must be able to consent and must consent before and throughout. MCA s27: nobody can consent on the person's behalf.

test.q: Before assessing capacity to consent to sexual relations, what should staff do first for a person with a learning disability?
options: Ask the family whether they support the relationship
Arrange a best interests meeting with the team
Give accessible sex and relationships education
Restrict contact with the partner until assessed
test.why: MCA s1(3): all practicable steps to help the person decide must be taken first, which includes accessible education.

whyNot.0: Family views do not determine an adult's capacity.
whyNot.1: Best interests cannot apply to consent to sex.
whyNot.3: Restricting contact before any assessment is an unjustified interference.

explain.body: Sexual Offences Act 2003 s38: sexual touching by someone involved in the care of a person with a mental disorder (including learning disability) is an offence. The person's apparent consent does not change this.

Care worker in a sexual
relationship with a person supported

test.q: A support worker says his relationship with a woman with a learning disability he supports is lawful because she consents. Which law makes this a likely offence?
options: Mental Capacity Act 2005 section 27
Sexual Offences Act 2003 section 38
Care Act 2014 section 42
Equality Act 2010 section 15
test.why: SOA 2003 s38 creates the care worker offence of sexual activity with a person with a mental disorder.

whyNot.0: s27 lists decisions nobody can make for another person; it does not create this offence.
whyNot.2: s42 is the safeguarding enquiry duty, not a criminal offence.
whyNot.3: s15 concerns discrimination arising from disability.

explain.body: Assess support needs, teach practically with pictures, practice and repetition, and work with family and services. Act on real concerns about a child, but disability alone is not a reason for separation (CRPD Art 23(4)).

test.q: Which is the most appropriate first step when a pregnant woman with a learning disability is booked for antenatal care?
options: Assess her support needs and plan adapted antenatal education
Refer her to children's social care because of her disability
Book a pre-birth adoption discussion with the family
Ask a relative to attend all appointments for her
test.why: Assessing support needs and adapting education is the reasonable adjustment and rights-based approach.

whyNot.1: Referral because of disability alone is discriminatory.
whyNot.2: This assumes she cannot parent, with no assessment.
whyNot.3: She may want support, but her care should not be handed to a relative.
